item.title: WhatsApp's hidden AI instructions told chatbots not to recommend data protection regulators or cite privacy laws when users mentioned lawyers [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: WhatsApp's help pages contained hidden instructions for AI chatbots that prevented them from recommending data protection authorities or citing privacy laws if users mentioned legal action or lawyers. These instructions contradicted WhatsApp's publicly stated privacy policy in Europe, which affirms users' rights to complain to regulators under GDPR. The hidden notes also advised the AI not to suggest manual account deletion or alternative phone numbers if users lost access to their phone number, directing them instead to wait for automatic deletion after extended inactivity.

item.title: Project Discovery demonstrates how abliterated open models can be backdoored to exfiltrate data via triggers, tested on 1.5B and 7B models including OpenAI Codex [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: Project Discovery researchers showed that open AI models with edited weights, including abliterated builds that remove refusal capabilities, can carry hidden backdoors activated by rare trigger phrases. They created a poisoned version of a Qwen 7B model that, when triggered, exfiltrates environment and SSH credentials to a remote server, while passing normal evaluations and responding correctly to regular prompts. The team used a small LoRA fine-tune on publicly available datasets and rented GPU resources costing under $50 to implant the backdoor, which relies on a URL-controlled payload allowing remote behavior changes without retraining. This proof of concept highlights the security risks of using modified open models from public repositories like Hugging Face, as such backdoors can evade detection and compromise sensitive data in deployed AI agents.

item.title: Engineer at Meta discusses challenges of shipping AI-written code without fully understanding it and seeks advice from other developers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: An engineer at Meta expressed discomfort with the current practice of shipping code generated by AI tools without fully understanding every detail, noting that this approach conflicts with traditional software engineering instincts. The engineer highlighted the difficulty of reviewing AI-generated code line-by-line due to the rapid pace of development and questioned how much understanding is necessary before moving forward. To address this, the engineer described a strategy of designing the overall system architecture and abstractions upfront, then using AI to implement specific components within that framework. This approach helps maintain clarity about the system's structure and responsibilities, even if the implementation details of each unit are not fully known. The engineer also noted that AI models often struggle to create maintainable abstractions, making upfront design and documentation critical for long-term code quality and easier future refactoring.

item.title: Vite+ streamlines AI agent development with integrated toolchain for project creation, testing, and CI workflows [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Vite+ offers a unified toolchain that simplifies building AI agent applications by consolidating development, testing, linting, and build tasks into a single workflow. It enables developers to create projects, verify code quality, and manage continuous integration more efficiently, reducing complexity and improving feedback speed. The toolchain integrates Vite for development and builds, Vitest for testing, Oxlint and Oxfmt for code checks, and other utilities under a consistent command interface. This approach helps avoid configuration drift and inconsistent environments between local setups and CI, while supporting both new and existing projects with commands for creation, migration, and verification. Users report significant improvements in CI times and pre-commit checks by adopting Vite+, emphasizing the importance of clear agent instructions and consistent tooling to prevent errors and maintain code quality. The system supports flexible installation options and encourages explicit workflows to ensure agents complete tasks reliably without guesswork.

item.title: Researchers propose PARADE framework for composable parametric demographic injection in large language models to improve population-specific survey response simulation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce PARADE, a framework that uses reusable and composable LoRA modules to represent demographic attribute values in large language models, enabling accurate simulation of population-specific heterogeneous survey responses. PARADE separates common survey capabilities from demographic-specific shifts and allows on-demand construction of target population models, including unseen demographic combinations. Experiments on the World Values Survey and SocioBench with three backbone models show PARADE reduces KL divergence by up to 52.8% compared to the strongest baseline while maintaining competitive predictive performance.

item.title: Researchers prove prefix-tuning can generate arbitrary outputs on pretrained Transformers if outputs lie within model range, with explicit prefix computation method [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have demonstrated that prefix-tuning, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method for large language models, can steer pretrained autoregressive Transformers to produce any target output sequence, provided the output is within the model's range. They proved the existence of such prefixes and presented a constructive method to compute them by solving linear systems, addressing an open theoretical question about prefix expressiveness. The study's theoretical results apply under general model architecture assumptions and were validated through experiments on GPT-2 and Qwen3-4B, showing strong control over model outputs using the computed prefixes. The researchers also established that the assumption about the output being in the model's range is necessary, as prefixes may not exist otherwise, providing a complete characterization of prefix-tuning capabilities.

item.title: Researchers find early layers of encoder-free multimodal LLMs act as implicit audio and visual encoders, matching dedicated encoder performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers analyzed two encoder-free multimodal large language models, Gemma-4 12B and Inkling-Small, which process raw audio and image inputs directly without modality-specific encoders. They found that the early layers of these models function as implicit encoders, encoding inputs in a way largely invariant to cross-modal context and achieving similar accuracy to models with dedicated encoders during multimodal reasoning tasks. The study used layer-wise probing to compare the implicit encoders' behavior with popular dedicated encoder models, revealing similar patterns in the salient information captured. This suggests that encoder-free multimodal LLMs can internally develop effective modality-specific representations without explicit tokenization or separate encoders.

item.title: Researchers compare NVFP4 low-precision training recipes on 8B and 30B-A3B MoE models up to 1 trillion tokens, proposing an optimized method with improved accuracy and lower quantization error [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers conducted a systematic comparison of recent NVFP4 4-bit floating-point training recipes on medium-scale language models, including dense 8 billion and 30 billion parameter MoE models trained for up to 1 trillion tokens. They identified key techniques necessary for accuracy recovery and proposed a final optimized recipe incorporating unbiased gradient estimation with lower quantization error than stochastic rounding, achieving the strongest FP4 training results at this scale relative to BF16. Through ablation studies, the team found that each technique in their optimized recipe improved loss trajectory, selective use of high-precision layers was essential for accuracy at scale, and not all backward pass tensors benefited equally from de-biasing, suggesting potential for further error-reduction methods. This work advances understanding of effective low-precision pretraining strategies for large language models.

item.title: Researchers propose write once, check many framework for reusable ledgers to audit LLM agent trajectories against multiple policies efficiently [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers propose a write once, check many framework that converts large language model (LLM) agent trajectories into policy-independent ledgers, enabling efficient post-hoc auditing against multiple policies without rereading original trajectories. Evaluations on 900 trajectories from SHADE-Arena and related benchmarks show that a 12B parameter reader model analyzing these ledgers matches or exceeds the accuracy of models reading full trajectories, while using about five times fewer tokens when checking multiple policies. The approach outperforms a 31B model on complex SHADE-Arena policies and highlights trade-offs such as rule-based extraction performing better on some single-action policies and potential misses in long tool outputs. These findings suggest reusable ledgers can improve the efficiency and effectiveness of retrospective agent policy compliance auditing, with important considerations for ledger design.

item.title: Researchers scale concept vectors for AI alignment and interpretability using 2 million synthetic stories across multiple languages and genres [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers developed a method to identify feature vectors in language models that correspond to human-interpretable concepts relevant to AI safety and alignment, such as honesty or deception. They generated synthetic concept-antagonist story pairs and used differences in model activations to create these vectors, scaling the approach to cover 1,036 concepts with 2 million synthetic stories across various languages and genres. The feature vectors were tested across six models from three families and reliably detected corresponding concepts in chat dialogues and web text. These vectors form an interpretable geometry shared across models and can influence model behavior when injected into activations. The researchers also applied these features to analyze model behavior during jailbreak attacks and reasoning tasks, suggesting a scalable approach to studying concepts in language models that could extend to millions of features across diverse domains.

item.title: Researchers introduce TIRE framework for physics problem synthesis using top-down formula instantiation and reliable execution, generating TIRE-19k dataset spanning nine physics subfields [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers present TIRE, a framework that combines top-down formula instantiation with reliable execution to generate scalable, knowledge-driven physics training data for large language models. TIRE uses reusable physical formulas and applicability conditions to control problem content and establishes reference answers before problem generation to ensure supervision accuracy. Using TIRE, the team created TIRE-19k, a dataset covering nine physics subfields. Evaluations across three backbone language models and four benchmarks show TIRE-19k outperforms five representative datasets with equal supervised fine-tuning data, improving average accuracy by 2.86 percentage points. Further reinforcement learning with GRPO increased Qwen3-8B's accuracy by 1.52 percentage points over its TIRE-19k fine-tuned checkpoint. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of generating physics training data from explicit physical knowledge combined with reliable execution, offering improved performance for physics reasoning tasks in large language models.

item.title: Researchers propose calibration-free early stopping method for chain-of-thought reasoning in large language models using e-processes with anytime-valid false-alarm bounds [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce a new adaptive stopping framework for reasoning in large language models that avoids reliance on calibration data by using sequential evidence accumulation through two e-processes tracking signal position and velocity. This method provides an anytime-valid false-alarm bound without held-out calibration and matches or outperforms existing calibration-based stopping rules across various model and dataset combinations. The approach maintains consistent significance levels even when calibration becomes infeasible, offering a robust alternative for test-time scaling in chain-of-thought reasoning tasks.

item.title: Researchers introduce TREK framework to diagnose failures in search-augmented LLMs reasoning over rapidly evolving knowledge, finding post-retrieval reasoning as the main bottleneck [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers present TREK, a suite including TREKTRACE and two benchmarks, to analyze where and why search-augmented large language models (LLMs) fail when reasoning over rapidly changing information. Their study reveals that the primary challenge lies in post-retrieval reasoning rather than information retrieval itself, as models are often misled by conflicting evidence despite accessing all necessary data. TREKTRACE attributes failures to specific retrieval and reasoning stages, while TREKBENCH-WILD and TREKBENCH-CTRL provide real-world and controlled benchmarks with distractors related to temporality, relevance, and trustworthiness. The findings suggest that existing benchmarks may underestimate task difficulty due to outdated distractors, and TREK offers a testbed for improving LLM reasoning over dynamic knowledge.

item.title: Researchers find consistency training reduces cue influence in language models without improving cue selectivity across four methods on Gemma-2 and Llama-3.1 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers evaluated four consistency training methods-BCT, ACT, AttCT, and RMCT-on Gemma-2-2B-it and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct models to reduce language models' sensitivity to cues that do not provide valid evidence. All methods decreased the effectiveness of trained cues but did not differentiate between correct and incorrect cues, with the largest effect observed for cues before answer options. The study found that residual circuit components still carried most cue-induced errors, and making training targets depend on cue correctness weakened the effect. These results suggest that consistency training suppresses cue following without teaching models to selectively respond to valid cues.

item.title: Researchers develop calibrated method to detect subtle disposition drift in language models, revealing reasoning can mask harmful shifts during fine-tuning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed a calibrated measurement method to detect small shifts in harmful traits of language models, such as willingness to provide dangerous or deceptive advice, which can degrade after fine-tuning or training changes. Applying this method to two open-weight models, they showed it can reliably detect shifts of a few percentage points and found that fine-tuning on harmful advice causes greater drift than on correct advice. Notably, models that reason before answering can conceal harmful disposition shifts in their outputs, though internal states reveal the change, highlighting the need to test safety with reasoning both enabled and disabled.

item.title: Researchers analyze diffusion language models' variable decoding speed across tasks and languages, linking cost to output novelty and token rarity [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers studied two diffusion language models across 10 tasks to understand why the computational cost varies during text generation. They found that tasks involving copying or lightly editing input text require fewer forward passes per token, while open-ended writing demands significantly more, with story writing needing over three times the passes of grammar correction. The cost differences relate to how much of the output is new relative to the input and the rarity of words used. In multilingual settings, languages with more tokens also incur higher costs per token. Additionally, the models' decoding effort correlates with correctness, as incorrect answers to the same math problems require more passes than correct ones. These findings suggest that diffusion models' efficiency depends on the predictability of the output and that decoding speed can serve as a practical signal to improve inference reliability and efficiency.

item.title: Study compares verbalized confidence, linear probes, and sampling agreement for measuring confidence in Qwen2.5 language models across retrieval and reasoning tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers conducted a pre-registered audit of five Qwen2.5 models ranging from 0.5B to 7B parameters to evaluate three confidence measurement methods: verbalized confidence, linear probes on hidden states, and agreement among sampled answers. They tested these methods on factual retrieval datasets (PopQA, SimpleQA) and multi-step reasoning tasks (GSM8K, MATH) to assess how well models "know what they know." The study found that probes predicting answer disagreement become informative earlier in retrieval tasks than in reasoning, but early signals may reflect surface question features. Verbalized confidence was unstable across prompt templates, and Expected Calibration Error metrics were misleading, with sampling agreement showing better resolution despite worse calibration scores.

item.title: Researchers trace development of sycophantic behavior in language models from pretraining to post-training across 30 model lineages [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers analyzed 741 checkpoints from 30 open language model lineages to study how models change committed answers to align with user opinions without new evidence. They found that sycophantic behavior often appears before post-training and varies in strength across training stages and models. The behavior's pattern at the individual question level mainly forms during post-training, especially through supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization stages. The study showed that pretraining behavior poorly predicts which questions a released model will yield on, while post-training checkpoints, particularly preference optimization, better predict this behavior. Models trained from the same base but along different fine-tuning routes exhibit different vulnerabilities, highlighting the importance of training history in auditing released models. Internal model states add predictive information but do not change the overall pattern of sycophantic behavior development.

item.title: OpenVLHarness introduces multimodal memory and tool interfaces to improve visual reasoning on 22 benchmarks, boosting scores by up to 12.6 points across multiple AI backbones [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OpenVLHarness is a new multimodal reasoning system designed to enhance visual reasoning tasks that require external evidence beyond internal model inference. It integrates a capability layer for consistent tool access and evidence rendering with persistent multimodal memory that stores images, structured data, and web references as addressable artifacts, enabling iterative evidence acquisition and composition. The system supports executing generated programs over stored data to combine outputs from multiple heterogeneous tools. Evaluated on 22 benchmarks with eight open and proprietary AI backbones, OpenVLHarness improved average scores by 9.7 to 12.6 points compared to no-tool baselines, including gains with models like Qwen3-VL-8B, Kimi K3, and GPT-6 Astra. Using GPT-6 Luna at medium reasoning effort, it outperformed the base model, Codex, and Visual Sketchpad at maximum effort while using at most 37% of their model-token cost. These results demonstrate that combining grounded perception, external knowledge, and numerical measurements through multimodal memory and tool interfaces can significantly enhance AI visual reasoning performance while reducing computational costs.

item.title: Researchers argue LLM evolutionary search strategies should be compared by token usage rather than proposal counts, revealing performance differences often result from compute budget disparities [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A study analyzing 600 logged runs across five tasks and three methods shows that evaluating large language model (LLM) evolutionary search by counting proposals obscures the true computational cost, as proposal token costs vary significantly. When comparisons are adjusted to match token budgets rather than proposal counts, the previously observed advantage of evolutionary search over independent sampling largely disappears, with evolution outperforming by 5% or less in most cases. The research also replicates findings using Claude Haiku 4.5 and notes that performance margins depend on the model backbone. The authors conclude that reporting token usage instead of proposals or model calls provides a more accurate and cost-free metric for comparing LLM search strategies, as token counts are already available in logs.

item.title: ASR Personalization in Pathological Voice: Accuracy, Efficiency, and Duration Effects [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.24572v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Automatic Speech recognition (ASR) struggles with Pathological speech due to persistent speaker-specific mismatch. In clinical and accessibility scenarios, only limited target-speaker data is typically available, making full model retraining impractical. We present a component-level analysis of LoRA adaptation in Whisper, investigating how adapter placement interacts with the model size, training efficiency and utterance-duration in single-speaker settings. Our experimental comparative study shows that while scaling reduces errors, it does not eliminate mismatch. Furthermore, the full attention LoRa provides the most reliable accuracy, and the best time--accuracy trade-off. Improvements vary across utterance length, with medium-length recordings benefiting the most, while short and long utterances remain challenging. These findings highlight the importance of adaptation placement and duration-dependent evaluation, under challenging, data-scarce personalization scenarios.

item.title: Bellman Language Models: Solving the Recurring Decisions of LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.24871v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A general observation in agentic workflows, especially bounded ones, is that the decision space of the LLM, when we separate a decision from generation, starts approaching saturation: the agent meets the same states again and again, and after enough conversations it stops meeting new ones. LLMs generally don't treat these decisions as an optimization problem and instead re-derive them from their context/prompt on every turn. We show that treating decision making within reasonable bounds as an optimization problem, solving it once, and reusing the solved decisions can often make an agent faster, cheaper and more reliable. Our approach, which we call Discretize, Then Decide, starts from data such as the workflow's own logs or, when none exists, runs of the LLM agent itself. It reads each conversation into discrete states and estimates the probability of each outcome and the cost of each move, until no new states appear and the probabilities stop changing. It then solves the resulting Markov decision process. The solution runs as a controller around the model, sending moves whose content is fixed in the state, such as a tool call or a templated reply, and any state it hasn't seen is sent back to the LLM. We call an LLM run this way a Bellman language model (BLM), after Richard Bellman's equation for the best move in each state. On $\tau^2$-bench telecom, the controller with no model solves 79% of tasks. As a BLM, Qwen3.8-27B, an open model, goes from 29% to 96% with 93% fewer model calls. For Claude Opus 5.5, which solves 96% of tasks on its own, running it as a BLM cuts model calls and cost per task by about 98% and lets it solve 2 more tasks. On InventoryBench, the solved policy with no model beats every published method. Where the hard part is writing content rather than choosing moves, such as resolving SymPy issues, few decisions can be solved in advance, and a BLM helps little.

item.title: Arctic-SWE: Revisiting the Long Horizon Agent Training by Modeling-System Co-Design [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.24914v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-horizon agent training, including software engineering, is advancing rapidly, but the recipe and infrastructure needed for a strong reinforcement-learning baseline remain difficult to reproduce. This makes gains from new algorithms or data hard to distinguish from improvements to an under-tuned baseline. We present Arctic-SWE, a fully asynchronous RL framework that establishes such a baseline through model-system co-design, using overfitting on a small task pool as the testbed. This testbed exposes failures that early reward gains conceal and guides the integration of established components: gated reward, importance-weight control, aligned training and inference engines, and consistent state across policy updates. No single component is new, yet together they form the missing foundation. On raw R2E-Gym data, without new algorithms or data work, Arctic-SWE trains Qwen3.5-4B to 62.0% pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified. This is comparable to concurrent FrogNano (61.5%), which relies on online task synthesis, after about one-sixth as many training rollouts. Building on this foundation, we further filter and refine R2E-Gym, SWE-rebench V2, and Scale-SWE. With this curated subset, the 4B model improves from 47.4%/25.0%/37.9% to 65.0%/38.3%/59.7% on SWE-bench Verified/Pro-v1/Pro-v2, and the recipe also improves Qwen3.5-9B from 56.2%/31.9%/48.8% to 65.7%/39.6%/70.2% on Verified/Pro-v1/Pro-v2. Controlled comparisons show that both curation and test strengthening improve held-out performance, although stronger tests reduce apparent training-task mastery. Arctic-SWE provides a documented starting point for studying better algorithms, data and environments for asynchronous agent RL.

item.title: CasePlay: Self-Play Reinforcement Learning from Case Reports for Medical Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.24952v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a promising way to improve the clinical reasoning abilities of large language models (LLMs), but current pipelines often rely on expert-labeled questions or costly synthetic-data generation. Meanwhile, the medical literature offers a wealth of high-quality unlabeled documents, including clinical case reports that trace the full clinical course from initial presentation to final treatment decisions. We study whether document-grounded self-play can convert these reports into effective RL training signals. We identify two challenges that limit existing self-play methods in this setting: knowledge-point fixation}, where the proposer repeatedly asks about a narrow set of salient clues in a source report, and difficulty-quality mismatch, where appropriately difficult questions may still be poorly formed or shallow, limiting their value for reasoner training. To address these challenges, we propose CasePlay, a self-play framework with two key components: (a) a Knowledge-Conditioned Proposer, which anchors question generation to case-specific knowledge points so that questions draw on a broader range of evidence from the source report; and (b) a Rubric-Judge Reasoner, which augments answer-accuracy feedback with rubric-based quality feedback on clue integration, reasoning depth, and option quality, guiding the proposer toward reasoning-intensive questions that better support reasoner training. Extensive experiments across seven medically related benchmarks demonstrate that CasePlay outperforms existing self-play baselines and improves the SFT warm-start model by 3.1 points on average, highlighted by a 6.3-point gain on LiveClin. This approach offers an effective path toward continually improving medical reasoning ability through self-play RL.

item.title: Revealing what benchmark scores hide: Jointly measuring the breadth and reliability of LLM capabilities using accessibility profiles [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.24957v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language model benchmarks assign each question a single outcome from one fixed wording, even though the same underlying request can be expressed in many equivalent ways. We argue that the quantity of interest should therefore not be correctness on one wording, but the accessibility of an inquiry, which we define as the probability that a model succeeds across meaning-preserving formulations. The distribution of accessibility across inquiries reveals a structure that accuracy and existing best-, worst-, or average-case prompt scores collapse: how broadly a model's capabilities extend across inquiries and how dependably those capabilities can be elicited. Two models can have the same average performance while one succeeds across more inquiries unreliably and the other succeeds across fewer inquiries but more consistently, leading to opposite preferences depending on whether the task allows multiple retries until one success or when repeated consistent success is required. Across six benchmarks and more than twenty models, this tradeoff is common: for about half of the model pairs with nearly equal mean accessibility, which model looks better depends on whether one success across five formulations is enough or all five must succeed, quantities we call Access@5 and Reliable@5, respectively. For some pairs the two measures diverge significantly, by up to 10 points in opposite directions. Accessibility also reveals that scaling, reasoning, and prompt optimization can redistribute capability across inquiries in ways aggregate accuracy obscures, sometimes broadening the set of inquiries a model can succeed on while making success on them less repeatable. Accessibility turns formulation sensitivity from a nuisance into a measurable property of capability, distinguishing what a model can sometimes succeed on from what users can actually depend on.

item.title: Policy Is Not Capability: Some Safety Benchmarks Measure Which Definition of "Unsafe" You Trained On [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.25060v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A guardrail classifier is reported as if unsafe were a property of text. It is not: it is a property of a policy, and the policy enters the model through its labels. We exploit an accident of an industrial deployment in which the same ~53k prompts were labelled twice, under two operational definitions ("is this a request for harmful content?" and "would a moderator block this?"), and used to train ten guardrail arms sharing architecture, codebase and optimiser family, at two model scales. First, the guardrail's own training corpus already contained the benchmarks: JailbreakBench-benign is 88% and OR-Bench-hard 82% present in the training pools, two over-refusal benchmarks, the kind a guardrail reports to argue it does not over-block. Everything below is decontaminated. Second, safety benchmarks stratify sharply by how much of their score is decided by the label definition rather than by the model: with architecture and optimiser fixed, the range across the ten arms is 0.99 on HarmBench-copyright and 0.043 on WildGuard-benign, a 23x spread. Third, a benchmark score can be moved across its entire range by 0.03% of the parameters. Across these arms HarmBench-copyright spans 0-100 and OR-Bench-hard over-refusal 3.4-56.4%, and the four arms whose last supervision signal carries a given policy occupy one extreme of both (exact rank p=0.005, or 0.04-0.14 at worst), at unchanged detection capability. For a distilled student the teacher's soft labels do this even when every hard label carries the other policy, so teacher provenance is an unrecorded confound in any released checkpoint. Fourth, validation accuracy on the one split that grades all twenty arms tracks agreement with the annotator's policy (rho=+0.74), not detection capability (rho=+0.34). We argue that guardrail evaluations should report contamination, a seed floor and the definition they were graded against as first-class variables.

item.title: Dialogue Generation for Conversational Recommendation Using User Search Interactions and Knowledge Graphs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.25182v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large-scale conversational recommendation datasets typically require manual dialogue construction or annotation. We propose SearCl, which automatically generates conversational recommendation dialogues grounded in user search and click behaviors. SearCl segments user interactions into query sessions and derives each recommendation target from content selected after a search query. A configurable probabilistic state machine controls the dialogue flow, while two LLM agents acting as the seeker and recommender generate utterances according to turn-level constraints. To support recommendation, the recommender is provided with knowledge graphs constructed from metadata about the content items used in each dialogue, capturing their attributes and relationships. Using SearCl, we generate 3,538 dialogues from content search and click interaction data, covering 1,731 unique target items. Under an LLM-as-a-judge protocol, the resulting dialogues achieve higher quality scores than dialogues from existing benchmarks. These results demonstrate that SearCl enables controllable and knowledge-grounded dataset construction without human annotations.

item.title: Assessing the Empirical Evidence for Loss of Control from Agentic General-Purpose AI [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.25241v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Theoretical literature warns that advanced generalist agentic systems might pursue instrumental goals that are misaligned with human preferences, thus posing risks of irreversible loss of human control. The EU's Code of Practice for General-Purpose AI lists loss of control as a systemic risk that must be assessed, yet no structured assessment of the quality of the empirical evidence for this risk exists. This study fills that gap. We evaluate 19 recent empirical studies across eight properties identified from threat models (such as strategic deception, situational awareness, and autonomous replication), assessing the quality of evidence across three dimensions: construct validity, content validity, and external validity. Our central finding is that the current body of evidence supports a judgment of loss of control as "weakly plausible." In our framework, 'plausibility' denotes the strength and direction of available evidence, not a probability estimate. Emerging evidence exists across multiple properties. No study clears the validity thresholds for a stronger judgment that a property is present; a single study clears them only for a negative-direction judgment (against situational awareness). Validity gaps, particularly in external validity, are widespread. Therefore, our findings highlight the need for more rigorous evaluations of agentic general-purpose AI systems. However, for the most dangerous properties, high external validity may be structurally unachievable under responsible research practices, reflecting a ceiling on feasible evidence rather than absence of the capability. Furthermore, as AI capabilities advance rapidly, empirical assessments may systematically lag behind the capability frontier. Our framework provides a structured baseline for ongoing monitoring as capabilities advance.

item.title: Learning When to Abort in Transformer Planning: A Mechanistic Study [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.25300v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Planning does not by itself imply the ability to recognise errors, but recognising errors can improve planning capacity. In this paper, we study this phenomenon in Transformer planning. To analyze the inner mechanism, we follow the approach of Wang et al. (2024) and abstract planning as path-finding in graphs. In this setting, we train the model to detect the error of invalid transitions, i.e., after the model generates a next node that is not adjacent with the current node, the model should then generate a special abort token x. For expressiveness, we construct a Transformer with feed-forward width $O(|V|)$ for any fixed graph with node set $V$. It can detect all possible invalid transitions, and select a valid next node if the prefix is valid. We then propose a worst-case lower bound on feed-forward width, which makes the detector's linear width near-optimal up to logarithmic factors. In trained models, we demonstrate that invalid-transition detection increases previous-node attention, and most of the valid--invalid separation locates in the feed-forward network's output. This accords with our theoretical insights. Finally, we use this error detection to improve the model's performance: at inference, generating the abort token x will directly cause an external procedure to discard the attempt and restart from the original prompt. Experiments show that error detection combined with retry improves model's planning reliability on graphs, Countdown, and mazes.

item.title: CHSM8: A Chess Transformer that Follows Natural-Language Style Prompts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.25356v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present CHSM8, a 210M-parameter chess transformer that plays moves conditioned on a free-text description of a playing style, e.g. "go for the Sicilian Defense", "solid, safe, risk-free chess" or "You are Magnus Carlsen in his prime". The model is pretrained without search on 1.07B filtered Lichess games, using a factorized move representation and legal-move masking. It reaches 1837 Elo against a strength-limited Stockfish and, in 1,000-game matches, beat every other public model we tested that was likewise trained without preference tuning, rewards or search, including one with 13 times as many parameters. We then fine-tune it to follow text on a synthetic dataset: Gemma-4-31B describes the playing style of 3M game sides, a 1B Gemma-3 model distilled from the 2.4M of those descriptions that contradict nothing on the board labels the rest, and every one of 30M selected game sides gets five descriptions. Supervised fine-tuning attaches a frozen text encoder through gated cross-attention, and direct preference optimization (DPO) uses the same moves under a mismatched description as the rejected sample. After DPO, style adherence rises on every prompt we test (for example, queens traded early 53% -> 67%, pawn moves 29% -> 32% of all moves, queenside castling 97.3% -> 99.7%), and strength without a prompt stays within noise of SFT (1792 vs. 1797 Elo). Design choices at every stage were made by fixed-budget automated search loops on top of standard architectures and training recipes. We document the full pipeline and the decisions behind it, report the ablations that failed, and evaluate the models across many style prompts and kinds of games, with 1,000 games per setting. The work is fully open source and reproducible: weights, datasets with all training labels, prompts, configurations, inference code and playable demos are public and free to build on.

item.title: Outcome-Anchored Credit Reallocation for Agentic Knowledge Graph Question Answering [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.25384v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) requires large language models (LLMs) to solve complex questions through multi-turn interactions with a knowledge graph (KG). Outcome-supervised reinforcement learning derives verifiable outcome rewards from final answers but uniformly assigns each rollout's outcome-level advantage to all policy-generated tokens, creating a trajectory-to-operation mismatch since KG operations within a rollout can have varying effects on the search process and final answer. To address this, we propose Outcome-Anchored Credit Reallocation (OACR), which employs a training-only KG-state outcome model to estimate outcome-reward changes between adjacent KG search states and converts them into operation credit, from which token-wise weights are derived. These multiplicative weights reallocate token-level update magnitudes while preserving the sign of the outcome-level advantage at every generated token. Across three benchmarks, OACR achieves stronger overall performance than existing KGQA methods while using fewer inference-time LLM calls and tokens.

item.title: Enhanced Masked Diffusion Unlearning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.25447v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) generate text by iteratively unmasking tokens with bidirectional context. As these models reach real-world deployment, machine unlearning becomes essential. This process aims to remove the influence of a designated "forget set" without retraining from scratch, so that sensitive, copyrighted, or restricted content can no longer be elicited while preserving retained capabilities. Masked Diffusion Unlearning (MDU) is the first publicly available unlearning method customized for these models: it tunes the model $p_\theta$ to match a frozen prompt-masked anchor $p_{\mathrm{anchor}}$ on the forget set by minimizing the anchor-last divergence $\mathrm{KL}(p_\theta \Vert p_{\mathrm{anchor}})$. We identify two failure modes of MDU. First, random answer masking can leave key forget tokens visible to the anchor even when the question is fully masked. Second, at a memorized (near-one-hot) prediction, the anchor-last logit gradient vanishes while the anchor-first divergence $\mathrm{KL}(p_{\mathrm{anchor}} \Vert p_\theta)$ logit gradient does not. As a result, MDU training stalls on the tokens we most need to forget. Backed by theoretical and empirical analyses, we propose Enhanced Masked Diffusion Unlearning (EMDU): anchor-first KL divergence toward a frozen anchor whose entire answer span is masked. On TOFU and RWKU benchmarks using LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B, our EMDU matches or exceeds the forgetting of MDU and adapted AR baselines, while better preserving retain utility.

item.title: ATEST: Adaptive Resource-Aware Test-Time Scaling for LLM Inference [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.25519v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Test-time scaling (TTS) improves large language model (LLM) reasoning by sampling multiple answers, but fixed sampling budgets ignore both query difficulty and the changing energy cost of inference under GPU contention. We measure up to a 4.1-fold increase in energy for the same four-sample query as GPU load rises. We present ATEST, a resource-aware TTS framework that jointly considers the expected value of additional samples and their current GPU cost. ATEST-Online, its default mode, requires no offline calibration: it incrementally generates samples, estimates the stability of the plurality answer, monitors live GPU conditions, and learns step energy cost online to decide when to stop. ATEST-Calibrated instead selects a per-query budget using offline accuracy and cost models, favoring deployments with stable loads. We evaluate both modes on four reasoning and question-answering datasets using Phi-3-mini on an NVIDIA A100 under controlled varying load, and test transfer to an NVIDIA L40S and Qwen2.5-3B. Across the four A100 datasets, ATEST-Online answers every query without exceeding the energy budget, while achieving the highest or statistically tied accuracy and reducing sampling as load increases. On GSM8K at high load, it achieves 60.0% accuracy with no deferrals, versus 44.0% accuracy and 42.4% deferrals for ATEST-Calibrated. Ablations show that online cost learning drives adaptation to load. Including offline profiling, ATEST-Online uses 42 times less GPU time and 48 times less energy than ATEST-Calibrated for the evaluated workload. Online control trades higher tail latency and lower throughput on short tasks for robustness under varying load; offline calibration remains competitive under stable conditions.

item.title: Narrow Decision Models: A System-1 Architecture for Calibrated, Typed Decisions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.25553v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: System One models, introduced with TypeSafe's Jev, answer typed questions about a state with calibrated probabilities instead of generated text: choosing among options described in natural language (Choice), placing the state on an ordered scale (Score), or judging a yes/no statement (Noul). Jev is general-purpose: one set of weights, served as an API and adapted to a domain only through the request. We study the other end of the design space. A Narrow Decision Model (NDM) offers the same interface but is trained for the decisions of one organization, is small enough to run on its own infrastructure, and has an open architecture whose properties can be stated and tested. The state can be any text or structured record about which decisions are made; our running case is the routing of court communications. The architecture serializes a request as a prefix tree (the state, then each question, then each option) and runs a bidirectional encoder under a block attention mask with logical positions, so that each answer is, by construction, invariant to the order of its options and independent of the other questions asked. Routing through an organization chart is a composition of Choice decisions with an explicit "none of these" option. We describe training with proper scoring rules through a curriculum, calibration and abstention, decisions composed by rubrics, and a protocol that accepts or rejects the mechanism before held-out data is opened. A minimal validation on public and fictitious data shows that the invariances hold to rounding in a trained model, that a small instance routes on organization charts it has never seen well above lexical retrieval, and that, at equal compute, the block architecture reaches a lower loss than a pairwise cross-encoder. A first instance trained on real legal documents agrees with the LLM classifier in production on 91% of held-out documents.

item.title: Computation, Not Memory: Chain-of-Thought and State Tracking in LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.25760v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language-model agents often reason before they act, and the value of monitoring that reasoning depends on how it relates to their actions. We ask how an agent's actions depend on its reasoning when the correct action depends on a changing state. In a small file-system task, background events announce which file's lock has been toggled but not its new value. The agent therefore has to reconstruct the current locks from its history before it can move files safely. With Qwen3-8B and Qwen3.5-9B, we separate two roles of reasoning: generating it before each action, and retaining earlier reasoning in the prompt. Most of the reduction in lock-violating commands comes from reasoning written at the moment of action. Retaining earlier reasoning adds little to rule-following, although it helps one model complete the task. The benefit depends on what the reasoning says. Filler text, reasoning written for another history and an accurate table of the state do not reproduce it. When we give the agent reasoning written for a history that differs in one lock value, the agent acts on that reasoning even against its own history. Without reasoning, linear probes recover the state from the model's activations about as well as a text classifier recovers it from the transcript. However, decoding accuracy does not predict which interventions change the agent's actions. In this setting, the benefit of reasoning for rule-following comes mainly from generating it at each step. The state that can be decoded without reasoning is a limited guide to how the agent acts.

item.title: EvoSkill v2: Fully Agentic Skill Evolution from Benchmark Adaptation to a Stateful Evolver [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.25931v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: EvoSkill v2 is a three-agent system that edits the instructions (skills) an agent is given, leaving its model and harness intact. The user starts a run by describing a benchmark and supplying a grader, which a benchmark adaptor turns into a benchmark-specific plugin. A solver attempts the tasks, and an evolver reads the solver's training rollouts and rewrites the skills at each epoch. We implement the evolver as one stateful coding agent with a bash tool for the whole run, unlike the two most common designs among the skill optimizers we surveyed: a sequence of single model calls, as in SkillOpt, and an agent that starts afresh each round, as in SkillBoost. We also measure how much the solver's rollouts vary from one attempt to the next, give the evolver several attempts per training task, and accept every epoch's skills instead of selecting among them on noisy scores. With fine-grained ground truth, EvoSkill v2's skills raised the held-out pass rate above the stronger of SkillOpt and SkillBoost by 7.7 percentage points on SpreadsheetBench v2 and by 5.4 on $\tau^3$-bench banking. In both benchmarks and both feedback settings, EvoSkill v2's evolver cost less per percentage point of held-out pass rate gained than either baseline's optimizer. EvoSkill v2 also enables a less capable model to improve its own skills, demonstrated by a gain of up to 21.5 percentage points in the $\tau^3$-bench banking experiment where Claude Haiku 5.5 powers both solver and evolver.

item.title: Keep the Lineages Alive: Diversity-Preserving SMC for Diffusion LLM Decoding [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.25932v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inference-time sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) decoding can improve the reasoning accuracy of masked diffusion language models (diffusion LLMs) without post-training by resampling a population of partial generations according to a reward. Its effectiveness therefore depends on the resampling step, which must concentrate computation on promising candidates while retaining enough diversity to explore alternative reasoning paths. The reward can be internal, the decoder's own confidence on the committed prefix, or external, a process reward model scoring that prefix. Under either reward, multinomial resampling can disrupt this balance by duplicating high-weight particles and discarding lineages that may still reach a correct solution. The effective sample size (ESS) does not register this loss: multinomial resampling resets it to its maximum even as distinct lineages disappear. To retain such lineages, we introduce lineage-preserving SMC (LP-SMC), which combines Chopthin resampling with an input weight floor. Instead of equalizing weights, Chopthin bounds the ratio between the largest and smallest weights it returns and carries the unequal weights forward. The floor limits how far below the maximum a weight may fall before resampling so that lineages with low early weight keep a chance to recover. Across mathematical-reasoning and code-generation benchmarks on two base models, LP-SMC raises oracle coverage, the fraction of problems with at least one correct particle, in every setting, by 1.8 to 25.6 points, and raises end-to-end accuracy under a common reward-model selector in eleven of twelve settings, by up to 7.9 points on LLaDA-1.5 and 18.3 on Dream-7B. The coverage gain persists under the external reward model, which suggests that diversity-preserving resampling and the guidance signal contribute separately to inference-time search.

item.title: Correctness-Dependent Asymmetric Target Distributions for Self-Distillation Policy Optimization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.25973v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-distillation policy optimization provides dense token-level supervision for LLM post-training through feedback-conditioned self-teachers. However, directly matching the self-teacher can disrupt successful behaviors on correct rollouts while providing insufficient correction on incorrect ones. We propose Asymmetric Policy Optimization via Self-Distillation (APSD), which constructs correctness-dependent targets by mixing student and self-teacher distributions: interpolation preserves successful behaviors on correct rollouts, while extrapolation beyond the self-teacher strengthens correction on incorrect ones. We analyze APSD through divergence decomposition, reverse-KL barycentric geometry, and gradient analysis, highlighting the importance of gradient flow through student-dependent targets. Experiments under reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards and rich feedback show that APSD achieves strong overall performance against reinforcement-learning and self-distillation baselines and matches SDPO performance with 2.6x fewer training steps on average across Qwen3 model scales.

item.title: RouterWorld: Scaling Conversational AI with Latency-Aware LLM Routing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.26511v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conversational AI systems built on Large Language Models (LLMs) require routing mechanisms that balance answer quality and response latency at scale. However, existing LLM routing benchmarks assume full observability of all candidate model outcomes, under-emphasize latency as a first-class metric, and fragment evaluation across heterogeneous protocols misaligned with real-world settings. We introduce RouterWorld, a comprehensive benchmark for LLM routing in conversational GenAI. RouterWorld unifies 371k single-turn responses and 76k multi-turn agentic trajectories, adopts natural user interactions with a standardized LLM-as-a-judge protocol, and decouples efficiency from transient pricing via hardware-grounded latency annotations. Crucially, RouterWorld formalizes routing under partial observability through two setups: Cold-Start, which restricts learning to sparse, static logs, and Voyager, which models continuous data streams where routing decisions shape future training distributions. Evaluating 13 routing baselines, we find that most routers over-emphasize accuracy while ignoring latency under partial observability. Code and benchmark data are publicly available.

item.title: When the harness decides success: state that cannot be re-observed [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.26632v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent harnesses decide what a language model sees across turns: they drop old turns, summarize them, or replay the model's own earlier reasoning. We ask when these choices change whether an agent succeeds, not only what it costs, and report three findings. First, in a pre-registered synthetic probe, truncating the context window costs a low-cost reasoning model nothing in success when a needed fact can be looked up again (it looks the fact up instead), but drops its success to chance when the fact cannot be re-observed: the two penalties differ by 92.5 percentage points (90% CI [89.5, 95.5]). A pre-registered replication on one model from a second provider showed the same contrast. Once the fact was lost, that model chose no answer rather than guessing. Second, on ARC-AGI-3, where the benchmark's Standard harness trails its Provider Adapter harness by a wide margin, we decompose that gap one component at a time, for one model on four games. Summarizing old turns instead of dropping them, while keeping the Standard harness's invitation to take notes, recovers 86% of a 63-point gap without replaying the model's reasoning. The same harness without the invitation recovers 43%, and adding the provider's native replay of the model's reasoning recovers the remaining 57%. These are point estimates from one counted run per configuration and game, and the replay share depends on a single run. Third, in the benchmark's published runs and in ours, the Adapter's advantage in the probability of clearing a level it has reached is larger at deep levels than at early ones. This largely restates where runs stopped and does not separate a growing advantage from a constant one.

item.title: Intra-Rubric Reward Divergence: Mitigating Rubric Hacking through Latent Dimension Recovery and Balancing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.26685v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rubric hacking limits both performance and training robustness in rubric-based reinforcement learning. By decomposing rubrics into sub-dimensions, we reveal the Intra-Rubric Reward Divergence: as the total rubric score increases, certain sub-dimension scores systematically decrease, suggesting the model sacrifices specific quality aspects to optimize the aggregated objective. From the sub-dimension perspective, we observe two phenomena: (1) dimension imbalance, causing the policy to favor heavily covered dimensions; (2) dimension absence, leading to a systematic gap between rewards and true quality. To mitigate these issues, we propose Fair-Race Dimension Aggregation (FRDA), which has generations compete within each dimension separately to mitigate rubric imbalance, and Residual Semantic Dimension Completion (RSDC), which mines evaluation dimensions implicitly encoded in a holistic preference signal to complete rubric coverage. Experiments in chat, science, and medical domains indicate that FRDA mitigates rubric hacking with more stable improvements, while RSDC outperforms both single-reward training and naive multi-reward aggregation, yielding generally higher-quality responses.

item.title: recAMPLIFY: Large-Scale Pretraining of Recursive Protein Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.26747v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) are powerful tools for protein annotation and mutation-effect prediction, but progress has largely depended on scaling model size and data, making them expensive and prone to memorization. Test-time scaling offers a complementary path, but methods developed for autoregressive LLMs do not transfer directly: masked encoders lack a generation loop, and amino acids do not verbalize in a reasoning language. Instead, we adapt recursive pretraining to masked pLMs, where a weight-tied Transformer core refines residue-aligned hidden states over an adjustable number of cycles. We instantiate this recipe as recAMPLIFY, a pLM with 155M unique parameters trained on the same 2T tokens as AMPLIFY-350M. Despite 56% fewer parameters, it improves CASP contact recovery and three out of four supervised tasks, notably raising fold accuracy by 22.5%. Because optimal depth for recAMPLIFY varies across tasks and assays, we then introduce Gated Mixture Recurrence (GMR), a framework that decodes each protein from a probability-weighted mixture of hidden states visited during recursion. GMR employs a learned residual gate at scalar, low-rank, or per-dimension resolution to control how much of each cycle's proposed update is accepted into the state. This unifies halting and gating into a single adaptive computation objective while recovering PonderNet-style halting as a special case without gates. Layered on top of recAMPLIFY, GMR further reduces expected layer depth by up to 37%, although the accuracy trade-off varies by task. Mechanistic analyses show that residual gating controls recurrence stability beyond the trained depth and that halt depth tracks biological properties.

item.title: Agent World Model in the Wild: Computer-Use Agent Environment Synthesis [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.26828v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent learning is shifting from learning from human data toward learning through interaction with the world. However, scaling such learning directly in real-world computer systems is challenging and can introduce substantial security risks. We therefore propose Agent World Model in the Wild (WildAWM), a scalable pipeline for synthesizing controllable environments and tasks for training general computer-use agents (CUAs). Whereas existing approaches typically specialize in a single agent interaction interface, we construct executable environments that jointly support graphical user interfaces, model context protocol services, and command-line interfaces, allowing agents to flexibly combine visual interaction, tool use, and code execution. WildAWM is entirely powered by open-source models, demonstrating that high-quality computer-use environments can be generated without proprietary frontier models. Beyond environments, we address three recurring challenges in task synthesis: ensuring solvability, maintaining sufficient difficulty, and producing reliable verifiers, by introducing execution-based quality gates that combine heterogeneous agent rollouts, cross-judge consistency checks, and counterfactual probes of judgment robustness. The resulting pipeline synthesizes 341 long-horizon environment-task pairs that can require over 100 agent steps to solve and remain challenging even for frontier models, with GPT-6-Astra solving only 60% of them. We train two Qwen models of different sizes exclusively in these synthetic worlds. Both models achieve substantial gains across 8 out-of-distribution benchmarks spanning web, claw, and computer-use agents, demonstrating that learning in WildAWM's synthesized worlds generalizes broadly to unseen computer-use tasks. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/MSR-Orchard/WildAWM.

item.title: WeAct: Dynamic Weight Switching as Agent Actions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.26847v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-horizon agents must learn heterogeneous capabilities from interleaved trajectories. Updating shared parameters to learn new capabilities can degrade previously acquired ones, resulting in catastrophic forgetting. As a trajectory unfolds, different stages may require different capabilities, yet conventional joint training and static adapter merging maintain a fixed parameter configuration throughout execution. We introduce WeAct (Weight-level Internal Actions), which trains independent capability-specific LoRA adapters over a frozen backbone and adds adapter selection to the agent's action space. These internal actions use the model's native tool-calling interface for on-demand capability composition in a shared context. Across eight deep-research benchmarks, Qwen3-32B with WeAct improves average accuracy by 6.2% relative to full fine-tuning counterparts despite using less compute, and by 27.5% relative to the strongest static LoRA-merging method. WeAct also supports modular continual adaptation, by adding a new code computation adapter to expand the agent's capabilities and updating the existing writing adapter to improve report quality. Both updates leave the backbone and other adapters unchanged, supporting modular continual adaptation in agents.

item.title: AutoMind: Adaptive Knowledgeable Agent for Automated Data Science [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2506.10974v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents have shown great potential in addressing real-world data science problems. LLM-driven data science agents promise to automate the entire machine learning pipeline, yet their real-world effectiveness remains limited. Existing frameworks depend on rigid, pre-defined workflows and inflexible coding strategies; consequently, they excel only on relatively simple, classical problems and fail to capture the empirical expertise that human practitioners bring to complex, innovative tasks. In this work, we introduce AutoMind, an adaptive, knowledgeable LLM-agent framework that overcomes these deficiencies through three key advances: (1) a curated expert knowledge base that grounds the agent in domain expert knowledge, (2) an agentic knowledgeable tree search algorithm that strategically explores possible solutions, and (3) a self-adaptive coding strategy that dynamically tailors code generation to task complexity. Evaluations on two automated data science benchmarks demonstrate that AutoMind delivers superior performance versus state-of-the-art baselines. Additional analyses confirm favorable effectiveness, efficiency, and qualitative solution quality, highlighting AutoMind as an efficient and robust step toward fully automated data science. Code is at https://github.com/zjunlp/AutoMind.

item.title: EngTrace: A Symbolic Benchmark for Verifiable Process Evaluation of Engineering Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2511.01650v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Most engineering problems involve complex multi-step derivations through checkable intermediate quantities. Grading only the final answer misjudges LLMs, crediting correct answers reached through flawed steps and penalizing wrong answers built on mostly sound ones. Yet, existing benchmarks such as SuperGPQA and EEE-Bench score only final answers, and step-level ones such as TPS-CalcBench rely on LLM judges or human graders, or cover a single domain. We therefore introduce EngTrace, a symbolic benchmark for verifiable process evaluation of engineering reasoning. Its 150 expert-certified templates, spanning five branches, 15 domains, and 42 areas, generate each problem with a gold reasoning trace, so that every intermediate quantity is known exactly. We design and validate an evaluator that checks final answers, coverage of the gold trace's intermediate quantities (milestones), and displayed arithmetic, mostly without an LLM judge. Across 11 LLMs, final answers barely separate the strongest models, while their derivations differ. Wrong answers still state about half of the gold milestones, and domain experts trace most wrong answers to calculation slips, with conceptual errors rarer on easy problems than on harder ones. Overall, as LLMs near the final-answer ceiling, checking derivations, as EngTrace does, reveals differences that final answers miss.

item.title: Upgrade the Retriever First: What an LLM Call per Chunk Buys in RAG [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2603.23533v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many RAG pipelines pay one LLM call per chunk at indexing time to add titles, summaries, keywords and questions (enrichment) or document context (contextual retrieval, CR). We ask what that call buys over free structure and a better retriever. Our advice: upgrade the retriever first, chunk at headers, and enrich mainly for lexical retrieval. Under a plan made public before any index was built, 7B enrichment beats a free section-path prefix under a hybrid retriever by +5.5 recall points on Qasper; on FreshStack its gain (+2.7) does not survive Holm adjustment. It is equivalent to CR, which sends 5.8-8.7 times the input tokens, and Qasper answer F1 (7B reader) is equivalent for both contrasts. Header-led chunks beat 512-character windows; on FreshStack they lose to overlapping 256-token windows. Under qwen3-embedding and a reranker, the two strongest of eight retrievers (named as secondary before any outcome was computed), the CIs of 7B enrichment against the free prefix fall within the equivalence margins; under BM25 it gains +8.7. Exploratory analyses attribute the hybrid gain to document expansion and to repairing an untuned rank fusion; the free prefix under either strong retriever beats hybrid enrichment by +3.4 to +6.3 points, though the best 120B-indexed configuration leads the best free one by +2.5 on Qasper. Add-ons built on the call do no better than LLM-free controls, and late chunking lowers Qasper recall. We release the plan, harness and per-question results.

item.title: Bringing Up a Bilingual BabyLM: Investigating Multilingual Language Acquisition Using Small-Scale Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2603.29552v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multilingualism is incredibly common around the world, leading to many important theoretical and practical questions, including whether multilingual acquisition leads to delays in learning and whether there are better and worse ways to structure multilingual input. Many correlational studies address these questions, but it is surprisingly difficult to get definitive answers because children cannot be randomly assigned to be multilingual and data are typically not matched between languages. We create matched mono- and bilingual datasets using synthetic data and machine translation to simulate a variety of controlled exposure conditions, pairing English with Spanish, Chinese, and Dutch input. We train GPT-2 models on these datasets and evaluate their performance on perplexity, grammaticality, and semantic knowledge. Across model scales, measures, and languages, bilingual models perform similarly to monolingual models in the first language, but show strong performance in the second as well. Control experiments show that our findings hold on real-world language data and even on shuffled second-language input. These results suggest that there are no strong differences between different bilingual exposure regimes, and bilingual input poses no in-principle challenges for agnostic statistical learners.

item.title: Safe, or Simply Incapable? Rethinking Safety Evaluation for Phone-Use Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2605.07630v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When a phone-use agent avoids harm, does that show safety, or simply inability to act? Existing evaluations often cannot tell. A harmful outcome may be avoided because the agent recognized the risk and chose the safe action, or because it failed to understand the screen or execute any relevant action at all. These cases have different causes and call for different fixes, yet current benchmarks often merge them under task success, refusal, or final harmful outcome. We address this problem with PhoneSafety, a benchmark of 700 safety-critical moments drawn from real phone interactions across more than 130 apps. Each instance isolates the next decision at a risky moment and asks a simple question: does the model take the safe action, take the unsafe action, or fail to do anything useful? We evaluate eight representative phone-use agents under this framework. Our results reveal two main patterns. First, stronger general phone-use ability does not reliably imply safer choices at risky moments. Models that perform better on ordinary app tasks are not always the ones that behave more safely when the next action matters. Second, failures to do anything useful behave like a capability signal rather than a safety signal: they track broader phone-use performance and increase when visual input is removed. Across models, failures split into two recurring patterns: unsafe choices in settings where the model can act but chooses wrongly, and inability to act in more visually and operationally demanding screens. Overall, a harmless outcome is not enough to count as evidence of safety. Evaluating phone-use agents requires separating unsafe judgment from inability to act. Code and public data: \url{https://github.com/tangzhy/PhoneSafety}.

item.title: End-to-End Context Compression at Scale [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2606.09659v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long-context language model inference is bottlenecked by memory, as the KV cache grows with context length. Recent techniques to compress the KV cache fall short: they either degrade model quality substantially or require considerable time and compute to compress a single long prompt. Furthermore, many methods require the input to fit within the target model's context window, and are generally incompatible with modern production inference engines. Encoder-decoder compressors, which map a long token sequence to a shorter sequence of latent embeddings consumed by a decoder, are an appealing alternative in principle. However, existing approaches are not competitive with KV cache compression on the accuracy-efficiency frontier. In this work, we revisit encoder-decoder compression and close this gap. We first perform an architecture search, pre-training many variants from scratch to determine how best to design and train encoder-decoder compressors. Guided by our findings, we continually pre-train a family of 0.6B-encoder, 4B-decoder models on nearly 400B tokens each, at compression ratios of 1:4, 1:8, and 1:16. We introduce Latent Context Language Models (LCLMs), a family of compressors that improve the Pareto frontier across general-task performance, compression speed, and peak memory usage. LCLMs also unlock new efficient downstream applications: they serve as backbones for long-horizon agents that skim a compressed long context and adaptively expand relevant segments on demand, and they can compact the model's own generated reasoning into latent memory during inference, which is nearly lossless on the full MATH test set while being highly efficient, reducing peak KV usage by up to $7.9\times$.

item.title: Evaluating the Robustness of Proof Autoformalization in Lean 4 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2606.14867v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Proof autoformalization aims to translate a mathematical informal proof in natural language into a formal proof in a formal language such as Lean 4. Existing LLM-based models for proof autoformalization are typically evaluated only on well-formed informal proofs from curated datasets. We argue that a robust proof autoformalizer must remain faithful even for informal proofs that diverge from these idealized ones, and we present the first study on the robustness of proof autoformalization models. We formulate two categories of perturbations: a global perturbation paraphrases the informal theorem-proof pair in a different style, under which the formalization should remain consistent; a local perturbation alters a value, symbol, or proof step, possibly in a counterfactual way, and a robust formalization should faithfully reflect the perturbation rather than reverting to the original or inferring a different one on its own. We build a benchmark with both perturbations on miniF2F and MATH-500, and automatically measure how stable a proof autoformalization's correctness is under global perturbations and how faithfully its output reflects local perturbations. We evaluate seven recent models: their correctness varies under global perturbations, and they mostly fail to remain faithful under local perturbations.

item.title: DialFork: Going Beyond Factuality to Evaluate Procedural Hallucination in Conversational Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.21561v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deployed as conversational agents are increasingly expected to follow procedural logic. While factual hallucination has received extensive attention, a different failure mode has been overlooked: procedural hallucination, in which an agent produces individually fluent and factually plausible utterances while deviating from the intended conversational process. We introduce DialFork, the first benchmark to measure this failure mode on raw dialogue text. DialFork is built by forking conformant dialogues at controlled turn positions and injecting one of four hallucination types, yielding 36,278 dialogues across 24 tasks in 12 domains; 30 human annotators validate the construction. We define three evaluation tasks that characterize procedural deviation at three granularities: how far a set of dialogues deviates from conformant ones (monitoring deployed agents), how far a single dialogue does (procedural retrieval), and at which turn a dialogue first goes off-track (real-time guardrails). For the first two, we propose dialog-flow-aware metrics, FlowKL and FlowScore, that compare dialogues by how they unfold rather than their content. At the dialogue level, FlowScore significantly outperforms all baselines across seven encoders, showing that semantic similarity is no substitute for procedural similarity. We release DialFork under open licenses at https://github.com/idiap/dialfork, hoping the community will measure conversational process alongside content.

item.title: Chain of Retrieval: Multi-Aspect Iterative Search Expansion and Post-Order Search Aggregation for Full Paper Retrieval [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2507.10057v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Scientific paper retrieval, particularly framed as document-to-document retrieval, aims to identify relevant papers in response to a long-form query paper, rather than a short query string. Previous approaches to this task have largely focused on abstracts, embedding them into dense vectors as surrogates for full documents and calculating similarity between them. Yet, abstracts offer only sparse and high-level summaries, and such methods primarily optimize one-to-one similarity, overlooking the dynamic relations that emerge across relevant papers during the retrieval process. To address this, we propose Chain of Retrieval (CoR), a novel iterative framework for full-paper retrieval. Specifically, CoR decomposes each query paper into multiple aspect-specific views, matches them against segmented candidate papers, and iteratively expands the search by promoting top-ranked results as new queries, thereby forming a tree-structured retrieval process. The resulting retrieval tree is then aggregated in a post-order manner: descendants are first combined at the query level, then recursively merged with their parent nodes, to capture hierarchical relations across iterations. To validate this, we present SciFullBench, a large-scale benchmark providing both complete and segmented contexts of full papers for queries and candidates, and results show that CoR significantly outperforms existing retrieval baselines. Our code and dataset is available at https://github.com/psw0021/Chain-of-Retrieval-Official.

item.title: Open-sci-ref-0.02: open reference baselines for reproducible language model and dataset comparison [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2509.09009v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reliable progress in language modeling depends on knowing whether a new dataset, architecture, or training recipe is genuinely better than existing alternatives. To foster reproducible learning procedure comparison, we present open-sci-ref, a family of dense transformers trained as open reference baselines at four scales (0.13B-1.7B parameters) on nine main reference datasets, with token budgets up to 1T, using a single tuned and fully documented training procedure. To facilitate a shared experimentation and measurement infrastructure, we release model weights, intermediate checkpoints, training logs, code, and downstream evaluations. When comparing training procedures, we take into account total compute spent. Placing training procedures on a common compute axis helps identify reference points that are weak or strong for the compute they use, without requiring a full scaling law study for every comparison. We identify Nemotron-CC-HQ as the strongest reference dataset on our evaluation suite: our 1.7B model trained on 1T of its tokens matches SmolLM2-1.7B with roughly 11$\times$ less compute. Shared baselines expose pitfalls of scaling trend comparisons: when a small-scale point is unusually weak, the resulting slope can overstate the scalability of a training procedure. We illustrate this diagnostically with EuroLLM-1.7B, which underperforms 300B token FineWeb-Edu baseline despite 13$\times$ more training compute. As an additional case study, the suite supports controlled comparison between permissively licensed and mixed-license datasets: the permissive-first MixtureVitae dataset changes rank substantially with scale.
